## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Uppādavāra* ("Origination Section", Ya 3.2.1) is a subsection of the *Yamaka*, the sixth book of the Theravāda Abhidhamma Piṭaka [SuttaCentral]. Within the *Yamaka*, the process division (*pavattivāra*) analyzes the condition of beings who are reborn or passing away in various planes and states [Anderson 1999]. This analysis is systematically organized into three sections: origination (*uppādavāra*), cessation (*nirodhavāra*), and combined origination and cessation (*uppādanirodhavāra*) [Anderson 1999; Ronkin 2005]. In the *Uppādavāra*, questions concerning the arising of phenomena are examined across time periods (present, past, and future) in both positive and negative formulations, structured systematically according to person (*puggala*), place (*okāsa*), and person and place jointly [Nyanatiloka 2007; Anderson 1999]. Scholars note that this process analysis represents early Buddhist process metaphysics and constitutes an important early stage in formulating temporal moments and the sub-moments of arising and destruction (*uppādakkhaṇa*, *bhaṅgakkhaṇa*) [Ronkin 2005].
SuttaCentral records one translation in one modern language for this text [SuttaCentral]. DharmaNexus identifies extensive Pali-internal text reuse comprising 40,232 matching passages across 50 Pali texts [DharmaNexus]. The highest volume of reuse occurs with corresponding *Uppādavāra* sections in other chapters of the *Yamaka*, especially Ya 10.2.1, Ya 2.2.1, Ya 6.2.1, Ya 9.2.1, and Ya 4.2.1, as well as its immediate companion sections *Nirodhavāra* (Ya 3.2.2) and *Uppādanirodhavāra* (Ya 3.2.3), and the *Pañcapakaraṇa-mūlaṭīkā* [DharmaNexus]. DharmaNexus also aligns passages machine-wise with various Sanskrit and Tibetan scholastic works, notably the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* and its subcommentary (*Tattvārthā*), the *Abhidharmasamuccayavyākhyā*, and Harivarman's *Satyasiddhiśāstra* [DharmaNexus].
